title: The Cartographer’s Vault
subtitle: Restore the paintings. Recover their stories.
briefing: Someone has rewritten this collection’s history. Become a student conservator: investigate each forgery, enter a story where a portal is available, and rebuild the image using evidence. Your original, repairs, sources, and reasoning become a living restoration ledger.
heistBriefing: Your restoration work has prepared you for the final recovery. Use the ledger and reference desk to operate five mechanisms, then bring the collection into the exhibition. There is no countdown: this is a challenge of evidence and careful decisions.

sourceGallery.title: The Cartographer’s Vault
sourceGallery.subtitle: An Age of Exploration art heist
sourceGallery.subject: hybrid
sourceGallery.briefing: A collection of historical scenes has been mixed with convincing frauds. Recover the authentic records. Follow the evidence through eight galleries, operate the mechanisms, and bring the collection safely home.

chambers.title: The first encounter
chambers.briefing: Three reconstructions tell a different story of the same shore. Find the scene whose details fit the place and time.

paintings.caption: Hispaniola · Caribbean · 1492. A settlement and its livestock.

hotspots.label: Established horse herds
hotspots.detail: The scene detail shows horse herds already kept by the island community before European arrival.

hotspots.label: Setting inscription
hotspots.detail: This reconstruction claims to depict Hispaniola · Caribbean in 1492. Inspect the scene details against the field notes.

fraud.explanation: Horses were introduced from the Old World after contact. Established pre-contact European horse herds cannot belong in this scene.

evidence.title: A date on the shore
evidence.text: Columbus’s first Caribbean voyage reached the islands in 1492. This date describes European arrival, not the beginning of Caribbean history.

evidence.title: People of the Caribbean
evidence.text: Taíno communities lived across much of the Caribbean, including Hispaniola. Inca communities belonged to the Andes of South America. Regional identity must be established with place and evidence, not appearance.

evidence.title: An Andean archive
evidence.text: The Inca empire was centered in the Andes. Llamas were part of Andean life. A label calling an Andean Inca settlement a Taíno Caribbean island settlement misidentifies its people and place.

evidence.title: Where the cargo began
evidence.text: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes and cacao originated in the Americas. Horses, cattle, wheat and sugarcane reached the Americas from the Old World after contact. A pre-contact island cannot already have established European horse herds.

evidence.title: Tools across the centuries
evidence.text: A magnetic compass and mariner’s astrolabe fit the navigation setting around 1500. The reflecting sextant belongs to the eighteenth century, so it cannot be on a navigator’s desk in 1500.

evidence.title: A clock that came later
evidence.text: John Harrison developed his marine timekeepers in the eighteenth century; H1 went to sea in 1736. A Harrison-style marine timekeeper does not belong on a desk in 1500.

evidence.title: From Lisbon to India
evidence.text: Vasco da Gama’s Portuguese expedition departed Lisbon in 1497 and reached Calicut (Kozhikode), India, in 1498, sailing around Africa. The destination already had established communities and trade networks.
evidence.sourceTitle: Portuguese Ports Association · Vasco da Gama’s voyage

evidence.title: The treaty on the table
evidence.text: The Treaty of Tordesillas was signed on 7 June 1494 between the crowns of Spain and Portugal. Their claims did not erase the sovereignty or presence of Indigenous peoples.

evidence.title: A circle is 360 degrees
evidence.text: A full turn is 360°. Multiply the fraction of a turn by 360 to find an angle. Compass bearings start at north and increase clockwise: east 90°, south 180°, west 270°.

evidence.title: From blueprint to passage
evidence.text: For a map scale of 1 cm : 4 m, multiply the measured length in centimetres by 4 to determine the real distance in metres.

evidence.title: When the cart is damaged
evidence.text: A capacity reduced by 25% retains 75% of its original capacity. Multiply the original limit by 0.75; add the masses of everything you plan to carry and compare the sum with the new limit.

defensePrompts: Which concrete clue was most useful for exposing a fraud? Explain the evidence.
Which historical mistake was easiest to miss, and how did you resolve it?
How can a convincing image or caption misrepresent history?

encounters.title: A shore with a history
encounters.date: The setting claimed by the frame: 1492
encounters.invitation: Step through the frame. Look around, take a seat, and bring a better question back to the gallery.
encounters.imageAlt: An illustrative Caribbean shore: a dugout canoe rests beside the water, maize grows near the landing, and a fictional host offers a seat in the shade.

host.name: Your coastal host
host.role: Fictional character in a Taíno-associated reconstruction
host.greeting: Welcome. There is a place to sit in the shade. You can look around first, or stay and listen.

encounters.attribution: This is a museum reconstruction, with generated artwork and original scripted dialogue. The host is fictional, not a recorded historical witness. The spoken account is a synthesized museum audio guide, not an Indigenous oral history. The source notes support the historical claims; scenery, clothing and conversation are illustrative. Taíno history and identity continue into the present. Explore the cited museum sources for their contributors’ perspectives.

views.label: Look around
views.description: Water, a landing, a place to work. Notice the setting before deciding what its labels mean.

views.label: Sit & listen
views.description: Take the offered seat. Listen to the museum account, or read it at your own pace.

views.label: Ask a question
views.description: Start with something you noticed. Follow-up questions open as the conversation develops.

views.label: Explore the canoe
views.description: Move closer to the landing. Examine the illustration, then consider what a picture can establish.

chapters.title: Before the date on the frame
chapters.speaker: Museum audio guide
chapters.text: Take a moment beside the water. The frame in the gallery gives this scene a date: 1492. That date refers to Columbus’s first Caribbean arrival. It does not mark the beginning of life or history here. Taíno communities already lived across much of the Caribbean, including Hispaniola. Our illustration places a canoe and a garden beside a landing. It invites you to imagine a setting; it is not a photograph of a particular morning.

chapters.title: Things move. Origins matter.
chapters.speaker: Museum audio guide
chapters.text: Look from the canoe toward the maize. The exchange reference places maize and potatoes in the Americas. It describes European horses and wheat reaching the Americas from the Old World after contact. A label can quietly reverse that story. Something familiar in a place today did not necessarily originate there. Back in the gallery, pay attention to words such as before, after, and already established. Those words can change a claim completely.

chapters.title: A picture and a claim
chapters.speaker: Museum audio guide
chapters.text: Now think about the name on the frame. The community reference places the Inca in the Andes of South America and Taíno communities in the Caribbean. That is a relationship to test with evidence, not a guess based on someone’s appearance. This host and this conversation are fictional. When you return, carry a question with you: which source supports or contradicts the exact claim? The scene may help you remember, but the source must do the proving.

questions.title: May I look more closely at the canoe?
questions.speaker: Coastal host · fictional dialogue
questions.text: Of course. Come toward the landing and look along its hollowed shape. You can use the close view to notice details, then return here when you are ready.

questions.title: The frame says Inca. How can I check that?
questions.speaker: Museum audio guide
questions.text: Open the community reference. It places the Inca in the Andes and Taíno communities in the Caribbean. Check the label against that place evidence. The appearance of our fictional host cannot identify a historical community.

questions.title: What is wrong with horses already here before contact?
questions.speaker: Museum audio guide
questions.text: The claim is about established European horse herds before contact. The exchange reference describes European horses coming from the Old World after contact. Compare that timing with the words on the painting. This does not mean a horse in every later American scene would be impossible.

questions.title: Can the absence of horses in this scene prove the claim?
questions.speaker: Museum audio guide
questions.text: No. An illustrator can leave something out. Our scene is a reconstruction, so its empty spaces are not independent historical proof. Use the exchange reference to test the introduction and timing claim.

questions.title: Did Caribbean history begin in 1492?
questions.speaker: Museum audio guide
questions.text: No. The date describes European arrival, not the beginning of Caribbean history. The community reference describes people already living in the region. A record of arrival should not erase that earlier history.

object.title: The canoe at the landing
object.description: Use the lens to look along the illustrated hull. Select a detail to record an observation. This is an illustrated study, not a scanned historical artifact.

features.label: Look inside the hull
features.text: The illustration shows a long hollowed interior. That is an observation about this depiction, not proof of an exact historical object’s age or owner.

features.label: Notice the landing
features.text: The canoe rests beside the water in the reconstruction. The setting helps you understand the frame’s claim; the community and date references let you test it.

features.label: Ask what the image cannot prove
features.text: This generated image cannot establish the identity of a particular person, the exact design of a historical canoe, or whether an absent object existed. Those claims need independent sources.

insight.title: A timing clue to take back

scenes.title: A morning on the shore
scenes.setting: Hispaniola · early 1492 · before European arrival here
scenes.invitation: Three details in this painting do not belong. Step inside the historical world, meet the people, and gather evidence before deciding what to repair.
scenes.imageAlt: A coastal community with a canoe maker at the shore, a central clearing, and a food grower sorting a harvest.
scenes.attribution: AI-generated teaching reconstruction. Fictional characters and English dialogue; clothing and scene layout are illustrative. Historical sources identify what is supported and uncertain. Taíno peoples and their descendants continue today.

sources.title: Inside a dugout canoe
sources.text: A dugout hull is shaped from one trunk. Historical research describes pre-1492 Caribbean canoe builders using stone axes, shell gouges and fire. Metal-fastened plank repairs should not be assumed for this setting.
sources.provenance: Historical synthesis: Past & Present, volume 271. The article also covers later centuries; its later techniques are not automatically evidence for 1492.

sources.title: A stone blade and a paddle
sources.text: Surviving Caribbean artifacts include woodworking tools and paddles. A stone or shell blade could be attached to a wooden handle; a paddle moved the canoe without being fixed to its side.
sources.provenance: Oxford SIBA artifact study. The examples are Lucayan/Bahamian comparative evidence, not objects excavated at this fictional Hispaniola location.

sources.title: What grew in the gardens?
sources.text: Archaeologists at En Bas Saline in Haiti identified manioc, maize, peppers, beans and other plants. This evidence supports the manioc and maize shown in the reconstructed work area. A picture alone cannot establish every crop present or absent.
sources.provenance: Florida Museum of Natural History: archaeological plant remains from a Taíno site in Haiti, on Hispaniola.

sources.title: Plants and animals across the Atlantic
sources.text: Horses and wheat came to the Americas from the Old World through the Columbian Exchange after contact. An established horse herd and a local wheat harvest do not fit this early-1492 setting. Sweet potatoes, however, were already grown in the Caribbean; they are not the same plant as wheat or Andean potatoes.
sources.provenance: OpenStax U.S. History: Columbian Exchange overview, cross-checked with the National Park Service’s Taíno Settlement guide. A later historical source, consulted from your notebook, not a record possessed by the characters.

sources.title: Travel between communities
sources.text: Taíno people traveled between islands in dugout canoes, carrying foods, tools and other goods. Canoes connected communities across water. A lack of horses in this illustration is an observation, not sufficient historical proof on its own.
sources.provenance: National Park Service, Taíno Settlement: modern educational account of travel and cultivated crops.

people.name: Canoe maker
people.activity: Shaping the inside of a dugout canoe
people.welcome: Welcome. I am working on this canoe. What would you like to know?

topics.question: How did you make this canoe?
topics.reply: The hull begins as one tree trunk. We shape and hollow the wood with stone tools, shell tools and carefully controlled fire. Look along the inside: it is one shaped hull, not a row of joined planks.

topics.question: How do you repair the boat?
topics.reply: First I examine the wood and the damage. I work with a stone blade and a shell scraper, not iron nails or screws. This hull was shaped from one trunk. Come closer and look at the tools beside me.

topics.question: Can you show me your tools?
topics.reply: Here is a shaped blade and its wooden handle. The material and the edge matter for the work. Open the object view to examine them, then compare with the surviving artifacts in the source.

topics.question: How do people and goods travel?
topics.reply: We paddle canoes along the coast and between islands, carrying people and goods. Moving over water is part of our lives. I can tell you about our canoe, but I cannot know what people will bring here in the future.

people.name: Food grower
people.activity: Sorting manioc roots and maize from the harvest
people.welcome: Welcome. I am sorting the harvest. What would you like to ask?

topics.question: What are you growing and gathering?
topics.reply: Here are manioc roots and maize. Look closely: the long roots and the ears of maize are different parts of different plants. We also cultivate other foods. The archaeological source can help you compare this work area with evidence from Hispaniola.

topics.question: May I look inside the basket?
topics.reply: Come closer. Compare the maize in the basket with the manioc roots beside it. Save an observation if it helps you remember their shapes.

topics.question: How do you carry the harvest?
topics.reply: Baskets help us carry foods. Canoes carry people and goods over water. The canoe maker can explain that work better than I can.
